message.content: Aluminum conducts heat faster, but conduction is about how quickly heat moves through metal, not how much heat the pan can hold. Cast iron wins on thermal mass. It’s much denser, and a typical cast-iron skillet is thicker and heavier than a thin aluminum pan. That extra mass stores more heat energy at a given temperature. So when you put a cold steak in a hot cast-iron skillet, the pan has a big reserve: it barely drops in temperature and keeps a hard sear going. A thin aluminum pan conducts heat into the steak quickly, but its small reservoir empties fast, so the pan cools and the steak may steam or gray before it browns. One limitation: this isn’t only about the metal. A thick aluminum pan, a heavy aluminum disk, or a large aluminum pot can store plenty of heat, while a paper-thin cast-iron pan would not. Cast iron also heats and cools slowly, which helps hold heat but makes quick temperature changes harder.
